defaults.permitted_development: Converting an existing residential cellar or basement in England is unlikely to need planning permission where the work stays internal, does not create a separate dwelling and does not materially alter the exterior. New excavation, lightwells or other visible external works can change that answer.

rules.height_rules: There is no separate basement height allowance. The planning issue is usually whether visible guards, railings, lightwell walls or linked above-ground structures become prominent externally.
rules.depth_rules: There is no standalone permitted development depth right for basement excavation. Digging down to create a new basement or materially enlarge one usually needs its own planning assessment, especially where the outside of the property changes.
rules.boundary_rules: Boundary-sensitive basement work needs careful review where it introduces lightwells, retaining walls, railings, drainage changes or substantial excavation close to adjoining structures.
rules.roof_rules: If the scheme also includes a rear extension, roof terrace, plant or roof alteration, those elements need their own planning assessment. A purely internal basement conversion does not usually create a separate roof issue.
rules.materials_rules: Visible elements such as front lightwell walls, railings, grilles, doors and paving should be designed as part of the existing house rather than as an awkward add-on. Heritage settings usually need the most restrained detailing.

rules.permitted_development: A straightforward basement conversion is often not a full planning matter if it reuses existing space and avoids significant external works. Excavation, front lightwells and creating a separate dwelling are the usual triggers for an application.

rules.height_rules: There is no single conversion height formula. The real issue is usually whether the project changes the scale or visible envelope of the building.
rules.depth_rules: Reusing existing built space is usually the simplest route. Excavation, extended footprint or enlarged floor area can change the answer quickly.
rules.boundary_rules: Boundary issues often come from external openings, excavation, parking loss or access changes. The simpler route is strongest where outside changes remain modest.
rules.roof_rules: Associated roof alterations should not be assumed to fall within the same route as the main conversion.
rules.materials_rules: Materials matter most where the conversion introduces a visible lightwell, new railings, altered windows or external grilles.

restrictions.conservation_area: Additional planning restrictions may apply in conservation areas.
restrictions.listed_building: Listed building consent is required for works affecting listed buildings.
restrictions.article4_notes: No borough-wide Article 4 note is recorded here, but site-specific directions or planning conditions can still remove permitted development rights on particular properties.

rules.height_rules: There is no single conversion height formula. The real issue is usually whether the project changes the scale or visible envelope of the building.
rules.depth_rules: Conversion that extends beyond the existing building envelope usually needs a fuller planning check.
rules.boundary_rules: Boundary issues often come from external openings, excavation, parking loss or access changes. The simpler route is strongest where outside changes remain modest.
rules.roof_rules: The conversion route does not automatically cover linked roof alterations. Dormers, rooflights, raised upstands and canopies should be checked under their own rules.
rules.materials_rules: External detailing is the key material issue here: the safer route is usually restrained lightwell, window and railing design that feels part of the original frontage.
